hormuz.label: Gulf shipping risk
hormuz.value: Gulf shipping risk persists despite diplomatic hopes

facts.text: Nov 5: new tanker attacks revived oil-supply fears. UKMTO reported at least five vessel incidents since Sunday in the Gulf.
Nov 6: Iran reportedly sent a nuclear proposal through Qatar, but still demands sanctions relief and an end to the US naval blockade before fully reopening Hormuz.

hormuz.say: Diplomacy has cut the oil risk premium, but attacks still threaten dependable shipping.

aicapex.label: AI capex boom
aicapex.value: AI investment needs cash, debt and equity

facts.text: Oct 29: Amazon kept 2026 cash capex guidance near $220B. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow was an outflow of $42.4B, largely reflecting AI investment.
Meta guides 2026 capex of $135–145B; Q3 free cash flow was negative $2.12B.
Oct 26: Meta launched approximately $35B of equity offerings, alongside plans for a future $60B at-the-market program.
Nov 2: Anthropic updated its IPO filing, reporting slower revenue growth and new risks to the computing capacity supporting its expansion.

aicapex.say: The builders are still investing heavily, but cash generation and financing terms matter as much as growth.

oil.label: Oil

facts.text: Nov 5 futures settlement: Brent $98.29 (+3.88% that day); WTI $90.52 (+2.72%), as new tanker attacks raised supply concerns.
Nov 6 snapshot: Trading Economics Brent CFD near $98; its commentary reports a weekly decline of over 12.5% as diplomatic hopes compete with shipping risks.

oil.say: Brent is near $98 after a large weekly fall, with tanker attacks still creating upside risk.

inflation.label: Inflation pressure
inflation.value: US Sept CPI 3.7%, PCE 3.6%; Canada CPI 3.1%

facts.text: September US CPI: 3.7% year over year; core 2.6%. Gasoline rose 9.1% in the month and accounted for over half the headline monthly increase.
September PCE inflation was 3.6% year over year; core PCE was 3.1%. Released Oct 29.
Nov 6 preliminary survey: Michigan year-ahead inflation expectations eased to 4.3% from 4.7% in October.
September Canadian CPI: 3.1% year over year; 2.2% excluding gasoline.

inflation.say: Energy still lifts headline inflation, even as household inflation expectations ease.

issuance.label: Bond supply
issuance.value: AI debt issuance plus $125B Treasury refunding

facts.text: Nov 3: Meta said it was raising $15B through a five-part US dollar bond offering to help finance AI infrastructure.
Nov 2: Alphabet sold €6B in bonds. Blackstone and banks agreed the prior week to $63B of financing for Broadcom hardware for Anthropic.
Nov 4: Treasury announced $125B of refunding securities, replacing about $97B of maturities and raising about $28B of new cash.
Treasury expects nominal coupon and floating-rate auction sizes to remain unchanged for the next several quarters.

issuance.say: AI borrowers keep issuing debt while Treasury rolls over maturities; gross issuance is not all new borrowing.

overcap.label: AI build-out risk
overcap.value: Investors question AI build-out pace and returns

facts.text: Nov 5: investors feared a Democratic-controlled Congress could slow data-center construction, triggering a sharp AI stock selloff.
Nov 3: JPMorgan vice chairman Daniel Pinto said AI revenue and earnings expectations were too steep and could correct.
Counterpoint: Blackstone president Jon Gray said compute demand still ran well ahead of supply; he also said higher capital costs would slow the pace.

overcap.say: Build-out and payoff fears are investor concerns; strong compute demand remains a counterpoint.

fed.label: Fed
fed.value: Oct 28 hold at 3.75–4.00%; next decision Dec 9

facts.text: Oct 28: the Fed held at 3.75–4.00%, by a 10–2 vote. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack preferred a quarter-point increase.
Nov 6: October payrolls rose 165,000 and unemployment was 4.1%.
Nov 6 after payrolls: CME pricing put a December hike near 80%, versus 66.9% on Thursday; Treasury yields rose.
The next scheduled FOMC decision is Dec 9, following the Dec 8–9 meeting.

fed.say: The Fed paused in October; stronger US jobs keep a December hike in play.

y10.label: US 10-yr yield

facts.text: FRED DGS10: 4.90% on Nov 4, compared with 4.95% on Nov 3. This is the latest observation displayed in the source at verification.
Nov 6: stronger-than-expected payrolls lifted Treasury yields and December Fed-hike pricing.
Bond supply can pressure yields, while risk-off demand can pull them down; the balance changes from day to day.

y10.say: The 10-year is below 5%, but stronger jobs keep upward pressure on rate expectations.

realy.label: Real yields

facts.text: FRED DFII10: 2.64% on Nov 4, versus 2.65% on Nov 3 and 2.60% on Oct 30.
Real yields remain a hurdle for assets that pay no income; a fall in nominal yields alone does not remove that hurdle.

realy.say: Real yields remain above 2.6%, so non-yielding assets still face an opportunity cost.

boc.label: Bank of Canada
boc.value: BoC hiked to 2.50%; October jobless rate 6.7%

facts.text: Oct 28: the BoC raised its overnight target by 25 bp to 2.50% to reduce the risk that high energy costs spread to other prices.
The BoC said further increases may be needed but it will proceed carefully. Next scheduled decision: Dec 9.
Nov 6 release: October employment was little changed (−4,700), while unemployment rose to 6.7% from 6.5%.
September CPI was 3.1%, or 2.2% excluding gasoline.

boc.say: Canada has already hiked, but weaker employment makes the next decision harder.

energy.label: Energy stocks

facts.text: Yahoo Finance performance overview: XLE year-to-date daily total return was 44.88%, as of Nov 4. This is not the separate month-end returns table.
Nov 6 FactSet: Q3 S&P 500 blended earnings growth was 31.4%, with 88% reported. Energy was among the sectors leading double-digit earnings growth.

energy.say: Energy is still ahead for the year, but the oil-price fall makes its future earnings tailwind less certain.

gold.label: Gold
gold.value: Gold ~$4,060 Nov 6 snapshot; weekly gain over 4%

facts.text: Nov 6 Trading Economics CFD snapshot: gold near $4,060 an ounce, down on the day but up over 4% for the week.
Gold fell after stronger US payrolls supported the dollar and Fed-hike expectations; safe-haven flows during the AI selloff supported its weekly gain.
Higher real yields raise the opportunity cost of holding gold, but safe-haven demand can offset this channel.

gold.say: Gold gained over the week, then gave some back as US jobs strengthened the dollar and hike expectations.

credit.label: High-yield credit

facts.text: Nov 5 ICE BofA HY OAS: 3.48%, up from 3.32% on Nov 4.
Nov 5 ICE BofA CCC-and-lower OAS: 13.20%, up from 12.97% on Nov 4, but below 13.27% on Oct 30.
Nov 3: Goldman CEO David Solomon said strong AI companies could still raise capital, but warned investors could lose money by picking wrong.

credit.say: Credit widened on the selloff; distinguish broad spread pressure from the weakest borrowers.

semis.label: Semis & tech

facts.text: SOX closes: 10,688.8 on Oct 30 and 9,390.2 on Nov 6, a calculated 12.1% weekly decline. The index rose 4.21% on Nov 6.
Nov 5: SOX fell 12.25%. Reuters linked the AI selloff to fears that the election outcome could slow the data-center build-out.

semis.say: Friday’s chip rebound recovered only part of a large weekly loss; regulatory fears now sit beside funding concerns.

cad.label: Canadian dollar

facts.text: Nov 6 snapshot: USD/CAD near 1.41 after weak Canadian jobs and stronger US employment increased the appeal of the US dollar.
The BoC raised rates to 2.50% on Oct 28, but employment was little changed in October and unemployment rose to 6.7%.
A higher Canadian rate can support CAD at the margin; US rate expectations and risk appetite can outweigh that support.

cad.say: The Canadian hike did not prevent a weaker loonie as US and Canadian jobs diverged.

sbcorr.label: Stock–bond corr.
sbcorr.value: Bonds cushioned the Nov 5 equity selloff

facts.text: Nov 5: the S&P 500 fell about 4.4% while short Treasury yields fell 12 bp. The curve bull-steepened during the tech selloff.
Nov 6: the FT reported stock declines generally coinciding with lower bond yields; a 12 bp rally since Nov 3 meant roughly 1% total return on 10-year bonds.
Nov 6: stronger payrolls lifted Treasury yields.
These are dated hedge observations, not a new rolling-correlation estimate. Bond protection depends on whether growth risk or inflation dominates.

sbcorr.say: Bonds helped during the equity shock, but strong jobs and inflation can still challenge that hedge.

factor.label: Quality > momentum

facts.text: October ETF returns: iShares MSCI USA Quality Factor (QUAL) +0.1%; iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor (MTUM) −10.5%, according to FactSet via MarketWatch.
MarketWatch reported investors favouring low debt and consistent earnings as AI stocks sold off in October.

factor.say: Quality held up better than momentum in October; treat that as a dated result, not a permanent relationship.

breadth.label: Equal vs cap weight

facts.text: 24/7 Wall St. put technology near 37% of S&P 500 market value in its Nov 3 report, explaining why tech weakness hurts cap weight more.
October leadership is a completed-month comparison, not evidence that every stock held up in the Nov 5 selloff.

breadth.say: Equal weight beat cap weight in October; that reduces concentration but does not remove market risk.

aipolicy.label: AI policy risk
aipolicy.value: Investors fear tighter AI infrastructure rules

facts.text: Nov 5: after the Democratic midterm sweep, investors feared Congress could slow the data-center build-out; the SOX fell about 12%.
This is a market assessment of future regulatory risk, not evidence that a new restriction has already taken effect.

aipolicy.say: The latest AI shock is a possible slowdown in data-center construction, priced before any new rules take effect.

chains.name: Is the bond hedge back?
chains.script: The bond hedge is working in risk-off episodes, but it is still conditional. Tanker attacks keep oil supply uncertain even after Brent fell toward $98. Energy feeds inflation, which keeps pressure on central banks: the Fed held in October but stronger US jobs put another hike back in focus. When inflation lifts yields, both stocks and bond prices can suffer. During the November tech shock, however, stocks fell while Treasury yields declined, cushioning portfolios. Strong payrolls then pushed yields higher again. I would retain some duration as a growth-risk hedge, while testing the portfolio separately against renewed oil inflation.

chains.name: Gold: haven versus rate risk
chains.script: Gold faces two competing forces. Tanker attacks can lift oil and headline inflation, keeping pressure on the Fed even after its October hold. Tighter policy can sustain real yields: the latest verified 10-year TIPS observation is 2.64%. That raises the opportunity cost of holding an asset with no coupon. Yet gold rose over the week as investors sought safety during the AI selloff, before strong US payrolls supported the dollar and hike expectations. Near $4,060, gold is responding to both haven demand and rates. I would watch real yields and the dollar alongside the oil headlines.

chains.name: Who funds the AI build-out?
chains.script: AI investment still needs external capital. Amazon guides roughly $220B of cash capex for the year, while its trailing free cash flow is negative. Meta is combining equity with debt, including a $15B dollar bond offering announced in November. Treasury refunding adds securities for investors to absorb, although refinancing maturities is not all new borrowing. This supply can pressure yields, but it did not prevent Treasuries from rallying during the tech selloff. Higher capital costs can then slow AI construction, while higher discount rates weigh on semiconductor valuations. I would compare funding costs and cash generation with demand before adding exposure; issuance alone does not explain daily yields.

chains.name: AI rules, chips and rotation
chains.script: The latest AI repricing reflects fears about the pace of the build-out. After the midterm sweep, investors worried that Congress could slow data-center construction. That reduced expected chip demand: the SOX lost about 12% on the main selloff day, then recovered only part of the move. Technology weakness matters more to cap-weighted indexes than equal weight. October already showed that distinction: RSP gained 4.95% while SPY fell 0.91%. The same month, quality held up better than momentum as investors sought lower debt and steadier earnings. I would reduce concentration and favour resilient balance sheets, while distinguishing feared regulation from rules actually in force.

chains.name: Oil's winners and Canada's bind
chains.script: Canada still faces a conflict between energy inflation and a weak labour market. XLE remains ahead for the year, illustrating the potential benefit of higher oil prices to producers. But energy also lifts inflation: Canadian headline CPI was 3.1%. The BoC responded by hiking to 2.50%, while October unemployment subsequently rose to 6.7%. A higher Canadian rate can support the loonie, but stronger US jobs and US rate expectations have outweighed that channel, leaving USD/CAD near 1.41. I would watch relative policy expectations and oil together; a Canadian hike alone is not a bullish currency signal.

chains.name: Rotation to quality
chains.script: Balance-sheet strength matters when financing costs and risk premiums stay high. Treasury yields remain close to 5%, and high-yield spreads widened to 3.48% during the equity selloff. CCC spreads also widened that day, though they remain below their late-October level. Higher refinancing costs leave weak borrowers less room for error, which makes low debt and dependable cash generation more valuable. October equity returns support that preference for the period: quality was roughly flat while momentum lost over 10%. I would apply the same balance-sheet discipline across credit and equities, without assuming that every quality stock or investment-grade AI borrower is cheap.
